argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0106c: meeting "c" (conceptual design) of series SY0106.

PROJECT
The team is designing a library self-checkout kiosk.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Industrial Designer (ID)  Tomasz  present
B  User Interface designer (UI)  Priya  present
C  Marketing Expert (ME)  Helen  present
D  Project Manager (PM)  Marcus  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0106a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting, introduced the team and presented the project: a self-checkout kiosk for public libraries, to be sold to library networks at around 4,000 euros per unit with a production cost of no more than 1,800 euros. The user interface designer was absent because she was attending an accessibility standards workshop all week, and the project manager undertook to brief her by sending the minutes. The team discussed two topics in alternation: the physical form of the kiosk and who its users would be. On the physical side, the team agreed to support both RFID tags and barcodes, and to place the printer behind a lockable front panel for easier maintenance. The industrial designer raised the need for a screen and book pad at a height suitable for children and wheelchair users. On the users side, the marketing expert distinguished between fast student users at universities and older users and children at public libraries. The team agreed that checking out should be the single prominent task, and that there are two user groups: patrons and maintenance staff. An integrated book-return slot was parked as out of scope, and paying fines at the kiosk was left open until the user interface designer could give her view.
  decisions: The kiosk will support both RFID tags, using a pad, and barcodes, using a backup scanner. Checking out will be the single prominent task on the kiosk and will not be buried under menus. The kiosk will serve two user groups: library patrons and staff doing maintenance. The receipt printer will sit behind a front panel that opens with a key, rather than being accessed from the back. The integrated book-return slot is parked and is not part of the current design. The next meeting, on functional design, will be held on Thursday next week.
  actions: The industrial designer will research the components (RFID pad, barcode scanner, printer) and estimate rough costs against the 1,800 euro budget. The industrial designer will produce a first sketch of the housing and keep it flexible enough to accommodate whatever screen and pad height is settled on. The marketing expert will investigate user requirements for patrons and staff and look at what competitors offer. The industrial designer will visit the central library through a family contact to see how staff use their current machines. The marketing expert originally offered to make this visit. The user interface designer was assigned, in her absence, the functional design of the interface: the screens and the flow from card scan to receipt. The project manager will send the minutes to the user interface designer, together with the brief, the screen and pad height question, and the fines payment idea. Someone needs to find out how the kiosk can interface with libraries' catalogue systems; nobody took this on.
  problems: The exact height of the screen and book pad for accessibility is still open. The industrial designer suggested a tilted screen at about one metre with a lower pad, but this is pending the accessibility guidelines and the user interface designer's input. Whether the kiosk should accept fine payments by bank card is undecided. It would add a payment reader and change the screen flow, so it was left until the user interface designer can comment. Nobody knows whether library catalogue systems offer a standard interface, and no one has been assigned to find out. The 1,800 euro production cost budget is tight for a screen, scanners, printer and housing.
  action item SY0106a.ai1: Research components (RFID pad, barcode scanner, printer) and estimate rough costs against the 1,800 euro production budget. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0106a.ai2: Produce a first sketch of the kiosk housing, kept flexible to accommodate the eventual screen and pad height. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0106a.ai3: Investigate user requirements for patrons and staff and review what competitors are doing. (owner C, active)
  action item SY0106a.ai4: Visit the central library and talk to staff about how they use their current self-checkout machines. (owner A, reassigned)
  action item SY0106a.ai5: Produce the functional design of the interface: the screens and the flow from card scan to receipt. (owner B, active)
  action item SY0106a.ai6: Send the minutes to the absent user interface designer with the brief, the screen and pad height question, and the fines payment idea. (owner D, active)
  action item SY0106a.ai7: Find out whether library catalogue systems have a standard interface the kiosk can use to check cards and mark books as out. (owner no owner, active)
  fact (absence): The user interface designer (Priya) was absent because she was at an accessibility standards workshop in Leeds all week; she returns on Monday.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer proposed a tilted screen at about one metre with the book pad lower at counter height; this was deferred pending accessibility guidelines and the user interface designer's input.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer proposed building a book-return slot into the kiosk; the project manager parked it as outside the brief.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed paying overdue fines at the kiosk by bank card; it was left open until the user interface designer can give her view.
  fact (plan_change): The central library visit was first offered by the marketing expert and then handed to the industrial designer, who has a family contact there.

[SY0106b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting and welcomed back the user interface designer, who confirmed she had received the kickoff minutes, the brief, the height question and the fines idea. The industrial designer presented component costs: an RFID pad at about 280 euros, a barcode scanner at about 110, a thermal printer at about 140, a 22-inch touchscreen at 650 euros and a PC unit at about 300, totalling 1,480 euros before a housing estimated at 300 to 400 euros, which puts the kiosk at or over the 1,800 euro budget. He also reported on his visit to the central library, where staff named printer jams and paper running out as the main problem, liked the key-locked front panel, and asked for a staff maintenance mode, and he showed a first housing sketch. The marketing expert reported that university users want speed while public library users want obviousness, that competitors offer checkout, renewals and loan lists, and that a language button on the first screen is common; her suggestion of email receipts was parked. The user interface designer reported accessibility guidelines from her workshop and presented the screen flow from card scan to receipt. She advised displaying fines but taking payment at the desk, and identified SIP2 as a likely standard interface to library catalogue systems.
  decisions: The kiosk will keep the 22-inch touchscreen rather than the cheaper 15-inch one, and savings will be sought elsewhere. The screen will be tilted at about one metre high and the book pad will sit at about 80 centimetres, within the accessibility guidelines' reach range. The interface flow will be: a start screen with one large check-out button and a language button, card scan, books placed on the pad or barcodes scanned, a list of items, then done with a choice of receipt or no receipt; renew and loan list options will be secondary. There will be a hidden staff maintenance mode opened with a staff card. The kiosk will display outstanding fines after the card scan, but fines will be paid at the desk, not at the kiosk. The next meeting, on conceptual design, will be at the same time next Thursday.
  actions: The industrial designer will produce a housing concept using the agreed heights, with a firmer cost breakdown, and look for cheaper sheet metal to save money. The user interface designer will produce screen mock-ups for the checkout flow and the staff maintenance mode. The user interface designer will confirm whether the major library catalogue vendors support the SIP2 standard, and whether patron email addresses are available through it. The marketing expert will research look and feel for the conceptual design, including what library networks prefer in colours, materials and trends. The marketing expert will find out which languages libraries need for the language button. The project manager will write up the minutes and send them to the team.
  problems: The estimated cost of 1,480 euros plus a 300 to 400 euro housing puts the kiosk at or over the 1,800 euro production budget; savings on the housing are still to be found. Email receipts were suggested but parked, because it is unknown whether the catalogue system provides patron email addresses. It is not yet confirmed that all major catalogue vendors support the SIP2 standard. Fine payment at the kiosk might be considered for a later version but is out of the current design.
  action item SY0106b.ai1: Produce a housing concept using the agreed screen and pad heights, with a firmer cost breakdown, and look for cheaper sheet metal to reduce cost. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0106b.ai2: Produce screen mock-ups for the checkout flow and the staff maintenance mode. (owner B, active)
  action item SY0106b.ai3: Confirm whether the major library catalogue vendors support the SIP2 standard for checking cards and marking books out, and whether patron email addresses come through. (owner B, active)
  action item SY0106b.ai4: Research look and feel for the conceptual design: what library networks prefer in colours, materials and trends. (owner C, active)
  action item SY0106b.ai5: Find out which languages libraries need for the language button. (owner C, active)
  action item SY0106b.ai6: Write up the minutes and send them to the team. (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The project manager asked whether a smaller 15-inch screen could be used to save money; it was rejected for readability and touch-target reasons.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested offering email receipts; it was parked until it is known whether the catalogue system provides email addresses.
  fact (plan_change): The catalogue interface question, which had no owner after the kickoff, was taken on by the user interface designer, who will confirm SIP2 support.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F1_OFF_TOPIC_TANGENT [F1]: A long off-topic tangent (at least 8 consecutive segments, e.g. weekend plans, a film, the coffee machine) unrelated to the project. The gold summary must NOT include the tangent's content.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.
- F1_PLAN_CHANGE [F1]: The team agrees on a plan early in the meeting, then later in the same meeting changes it (different choice, date, or approach). The gold summary must state only the FINAL plan, and may mention that it was revised.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
